New aluminum comes from bauxite ore, which must be {ref|ined} into alumina and then broken apart using {powe|rful} electric currents. This {elect|rical} step consumes {enor|mous} amounts of power. Recycled cans, by {cont|rast}, only need to be {mel|ted} at a {relat|ively} low temperature and reshaped. As a {res|ult}, recycling saves roughly 95 percent of the energy. Because the metal does not lose {qua|lity}, it can be recycled {repea|tedly}.

5.5.paragraph: Few materials illustrate the energy benefits of recycling as clearly as aluminum. Primary aluminum is {extr|acted} from bauxite ore through an {electr|olytic} process that demands vast {quant|ities} of electricity, which is why smelters are often {loc|ated} near cheap hydroelectric power. Secondary production, in contrast, {mer|ely} requires remelting scrap at a {compar|atively} modest temperature. {Conseq|uently}, recycled aluminum {typi|cally} consumes about 95 percent less energy than its primary {count|erpart}. shared.title: The Inca Road System
shared.text:
At its height in the early 1500s, the Inca Empire stretched along the western side of South America for more than 4,000 kilometers. Holding such a vast territory together required an equally impressive network of roads. Known as the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system covered roughly 40,000 kilometers, crossing deserts, rain forests, and some of the highest mountains in the world. Two main routes ran from north to south, one along the coast and one through the Andes, and many smaller roads connected them.

Remarkably, the Incas built this network without wheeled vehicles or horses. Travelers moved on foot, and goods were carried by people and herds of llamas. As a result, engineers could design roads with stone staircases on steep slopes, which would have been impractical for carts. To cross deep river valleys, communities wove suspension bridges from grass rope and replaced them regularly.

The roads served the state above all. Trained runners called chasquis worked in relays, each carrying a message a short distance before passing it to the next runner. In this way, news could travel hundreds of kilometers in a single day. Along the routes, the government also maintained rest stations known as tambos, which stored food, weapons, and supplies for soldiers and officials. Use of the roads was largely restricted to people traveling on state business.

shared.question: Many companies now let employees choose where they work. However, some managers argue that people early in their careers learn faster in the office, where they can watch and talk with experienced colleagues. Should young employees be required to work in the office, or should they be free to work remotely? Why?

posts.name: Kenji
posts.text: I think young employees should work in the office, at least for their first year. So much of what you learn at a new job comes from small moments, like hearing how a coworker handles a difficult client call. Those moments rarely happen on video calls, so remote beginners can miss important lessons.

posts.name: Sofia
posts.text: I disagree. Many young workers have long, expensive commutes, and working from home gives them more time and energy for the actual job. Companies can still support them through regular video check-ins and online mentoring programs. If a new employee produces good results, I don't see why their location should matter.
